nameStory: Tetraëdron gets its name from the Greek words 'tetra' meaning four and 'hedron' meaning face or side, referring to its distinctive four-sided geometric shape. When scientists first observed these tiny algae under microscopes in the 1800s, they were struck by how perfectly triangular and pyramid-like each cell appeared. The name 'minimum' simply means it's one of the smallest members of its genus.
description: Tetraëdron minimum is a microscopic freshwater alga that you'll never see with the naked eye - each cell is smaller than the width of a human hair. These tiny organisms are single-celled and have a distinctive triangular or pyramid shape when viewed under a microscope. They're part of the green algae family and contribute to the greenish tinge you might notice in pond water. Despite being invisible individually, they can form colonies that create visible patches of green in still water bodies.

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Individual cells are only 5-15 micrometers across - you'll need a microscope with at least 400x magnification to see their distinctive shape clearly

idTips.label: Triangular cell shape
idTips.description: Each cell forms a perfect three or four-sided pyramid shape with sharp corners, looking like tiny geometric crystals floating in the water

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Under the microscope, cells appear bright emerald green due to their chlorophyll, often with a slightly translucent quality

idTips.label: Solitary lifestyle
idTips.description: Unlike many algae, these cells typically float alone rather than forming chains or clusters, though you may find several in the same water sample

habitat: Look for Tetraëdron minimum in quiet freshwater environments like small ponds, slow-moving streams, and temporary pools throughout New England's forests and wetlands. It prefers nutrient-rich water and is often found in areas where fallen leaves or other organic matter have enriched the water. You're most likely to encounter it in shallow, sun-warmed water where other microscopic life is abundant.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to grow as water temperatures warm and daylight hours increase. This is often the best time to find them as spring runoff creates ideal nutrient conditions.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm months when photosynthesis is most active. Look for them in sun-warmed shallow areas of ponds and slow streams.
seasonality.fall: Numbers typically decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases, though they may persist in protected areas with warmer microclimates.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant or present in very low numbers. Some may survive as resistant stages in pond sediments until spring returns.

funFact: Despite being smaller than most bacteria, Tetraëdron minimum cells are actually more complex than bacterial cells - they have a true nucleus and tiny green factories called chloroplasts that let them make their own food from sunlight, just like giant trees do!
confusionNotes: Under the microscope, it's most easily confused with other small geometric algae like Scenedesmus, but Tetraëdron's pyramid shape with distinct corners sets it apart from the oval or spindle shapes of most other microscopic algae. Remember: if it looks like a tiny green pyramid or triangle, you've likely found a Tetraëdron.
contextualKnowledge: The observation count of only 6 in New England doesn't mean this species is rare - it simply reflects how few people actively study microscopic algae compared to larger plants. Many microscopic species are likely much more common than records suggest, but require specialized equipment and expertise to identify properly.
compareHints: Tetraëdron minimum is smaller and more delicate than its relative Tetraëdron caudatum, which has distinctive tail-like projections extending from its corners. While both share the characteristic geometric pyramid shape, T. minimum has clean, sharp edges without any extensions or spines. The 'minimum' species also tends to be more solitary, while caudatum sometimes forms loose associations with other cells.
